# Wisdom of Solomon Chapter 10 — Disagreement Log
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Date:** 2026-03-17

---

## Disagreement 1 — WIS 10:3: The death of Cain — "fratricidal rage" vs. "rage of brother-murder"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "he perished himself in the rage of brother-murder" |
| LOGOS | "he perished in the fratricidal rage that he himself had kindled" |
| PNEUMA | "he destroyed himself through the rage of murder — his own brother's blood on his hands" |

**Issue:** Greek orgē adelphoktanō — "rage of fratricidal [one]" or "rage of one who murders a brother." EMET is literal but hyphenated in an unusual way; LOGOS uses "fratricidal" (precise but somewhat learned); PNEUMA expands into a clause. The verse alludes to Cain without naming him. The author's point is that departure from Wisdom results in self-destruction: Cain's "perishing" may refer to his moral/spiritual ruin rather than physical death.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** "he perished in the fratricidal rage that he himself had kindled" (LOGOS). "Fratricidal" is the precise classical term for killing a brother; the relative clause "that he himself had kindled" makes explicit the self-caused nature of the ruin.

---

## Disagreement 2 — WIS 10:4: Noah's ark — "paltry wood" vs. "worthless timber" vs. "few planks"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "steering the righteous man through paltry wood" |
| LOGOS | "steering the righteous man to safety through worthless timber" |
| PNEUMA | "guided a righteous man to safety through a few planks of wood" |

**Issue:** Greek eutelous xylou — "of cheap/trifling wood." The point is the theological irony: such a flimsy vessel, yet it saves the world. EMET's "paltry" is good; LOGOS's "worthless timber" is accurate and ironic; PNEUMA's "few planks" loses the key qualifier (it was cheap/low-value, not necessarily few in number).

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** "steering the righteous man to safety through worthless timber" (LOGOS). The irony of deliverance-through-cheap-means is the theological point; "worthless timber" carries it better than "paltry wood" or "few planks."

---

## Disagreement 3 — WIS 10:5: Abraham and Isaac — "compassion for his child"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "kept him strong in the face-of compassion for [his] child" |
| LOGOS | "kept him resolute in the face of compassion for his child" |
| PNEUMA | "even when everything within him cried out to spare his son" |

**Issue:** Greek en splagchnois teknon — "in the bowels/affection of a child." Greek splagchna (bowels) was the seat of deep emotion — compassion, parental love. The verse alludes to the Aqedah (binding of Isaac) without naming it. EMET's "strong" is weaker than LOGOS's "resolute." PNEUMA dramatizes internally but departs significantly from the Greek.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** "kept him resolute in the face of compassion for his child" (LOGOS). "Resolute" captures the tested endurance; "compassion for his child" preserves the splagchna term's emotional weight without over-paraphrase.

---

## Disagreement 4 — WIS 10:7: Lot's wife — "a salt-standing-pillar" vs. "a pillar of salt"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "a salt-standing-pillar, a monument of an unbelieving soul" |
| LOGOS | "a pillar of salt standing there — a monument to a soul that did not believe" |
| PNEUMA | "a standing pillar of salt — a permanent monument to a woman who refused to trust" |

**Issue:** EMET preserves the compound Greek construction (stylos halōn) but the hyphenation is awkward. PNEUMA specifies "woman" (the referent is indeed Lot's wife) and adds "permanent" without warrant. LOGOS is clean and accurate.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** "a pillar of salt standing there — a monument to a soul that did not believe" (LOGOS). The deliberate anonymity of "a soul" is part of the author's consistent avoidance of proper names in ch. 10; PNEUMA's "a woman" breaks this literary pattern.

---

## Disagreement 5 — WIS 10:10: Jacob — "kingdom of God" and what it means

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "she showed him the kingdom of God" |
| LOGOS | "she showed him the kingdom of God" |
| PNEUMA | "She revealed to him the kingdom of God" |

**Issue:** All three agree on "kingdom of God" — but this is the only occurrence of the phrase "kingdom of God" (basileian theou) in the entire deuterocanon, and one of only a handful in the whole LXX. The referent is Jacob's theophany at Bethel (Gen 28:10-22) and Peniel (Gen 32:22-32). EMET and LOGOS use "showed"; PNEUMA uses "revealed." All are defensible.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** "she showed him the kingdom of God" (EMET/LOGOS). "Showed" is the more literal edeixen and carries the visual, theophanic character of the encounters. This phrase deserves a note for its theological significance.

---

## Disagreement 6 — WIS 10:14: Joseph — "pit" and the dual meaning

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "she went-down with him into a pit" |
| LOGOS | "she went down with him into a pit" |
| PNEUMA | "She went down into the pit with him" |

**Issue:** Greek lakkon means cistern/pit — the same term used in the LXX of Genesis for the pit Joseph was thrown into and the pit of the prison (cf. project convention: "pit" for bor in Joseph cycle). All three translators agree, which is consistent with established project convention.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** "she went down with him into a pit" (LOGOS/EMET) — unanimous. Consistent with established project convention for bor/lakkon in the Joseph cycle.

---

## Disagreement 7 — WIS 10:19: The Egyptians at the sea — "spewed them out" vs. "cast them up"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "from the depth of the abyss she spewed them out" |
| LOGOS | "from the depth of the abyss she cast them up" |
| PNEUMA | "cast them out from the deep abyss" |

**Issue:** Greek anebrase — "boiled up, spewed forth" — is a vivid word suggesting the sea convulsing. EMET's "spewed" preserves this visceral quality; LOGOS's "cast up" is more restrained; PNEUMA's "cast out" is spatially ambiguous.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** "from the depth of the abyss she cast them up" (LOGOS). While "spewed" captures the verb's force, "cast them up" is more dignified in context — the sea casting the enemy onto the shore aligns with the Exodus narrative.
